🔎 Introduction: what autocomplete does

Hinglish samajh: Search box mein type karte hi neeche jo suggestions aati hain use autocomplete (typeahead) kehte hain. System ka kaam: jaise hi user har akshar type kare, ab tak type kiye gaye prefix ke liye top k sabse popular suggestions bahut tezi se (lagbhag 100 ms mein) dena. Features: 5 results tak, popularity (frequency) ke hisaab se, sirf lowercase English letters, tez aur scalable. Hum trie data structure, caching, offline data processing aur sharding use karenge.

When you start typing in a search box and a list of suggestions appears under it, that is autocomplete (also called typeahead or incremental search). Type "tw" and you may see "twitter", "twitch", "twilight" and so on. Autocomplete saves typing, helps people spell, and guides them towards popular searches. It is used in Google, Amazon, YouTube and nearly every app that has a search box.

The task of the system is: as the user types each letter, return the top k most relevant suggestions for what has been typed so far (the prefix). The design question in this chapter is how to do this very fast (under about 100 milliseconds, otherwise the list lags behind the typing), for millions of users, using the history of what people have searched for.

The features we will build: suggest up to 5 results, ranked by popularity (how often the query was searched), support only lowercase English letters, and be fast and scalable. We will use a data structure called a trie, together with caching, offline data processing and sharding.

✨ Features

  • Real-time suggestions as the user types.
  • Top 5 results ranked by popularity.
  • Fast (under about 100 ms) and scalable.

✅ Benefits

  • Fewer keystrokes and fewer spelling mistakes.
  • Guides users to popular searches.
  • Improves the search experience.

⚠️ Problems

  • Every keystroke is a request, so the load is high.
  • Results must be nearly instant.
  • Suggestions can show unwanted or harmful queries if not filtered.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Introduction

Autocomplete, also known as typeahead or incremental search, provides real-time suggestions to users as they type in search boxes. The system must efficiently deliver top-k relevant and popular suggestions based on historical query data.

Key Features

  • Suggest up to 5 autocomplete results.
  • Based on query popularity (frequency).
  • Support only lowercase English characters.
  • Fast response time (<100 ms) and scalable.

Interview questions and answers

What is autocomplete?
A feature that shows suggested completions of a search query as the user types, usually the most popular matching queries.
What is the core design question?
How to return the top k popular suggestions for a prefix very fast, for millions of users.
Cross question: Why must the response be under 100 ms?
Because the user keeps typing. If a suggestion list arrives late, it is for an older prefix and feels laggy.
Cross question: Where does the ranking come from?
From the historical frequency of queries: how many times each query has been searched.

📏 Step 1: Requirements and estimation

Hinglish samajh: Requirements: real-time suggestions, top 5 results popularity ke hisaab se, 10 million DAU, high availability, aur roz lagbhag 0.4 GB naya data. Maanyatayein: har user roz 10 baar search karta hai, har query lagbhag 20 characters ki, aur har akshar par ek request jaati hai. Isse 2 billion requests per din, yaani lagbhag 24,000 QPS aur peak par lagbhag 48,000 QPS. Asli chunauti storage nahi, speed hai.

The requirements are: show relevant suggestions in real time as the user types; return the top 5 results sorted by popularity; support 10 million daily active users (DAU); stay highly available during failures; and handle a data growth of about 0.4 GB per day of new query data. We also keep the response time under about 100 milliseconds.

Where do the numbers come from? The standard assumptions (these are the usual textbook assumptions, shown here so you can reproduce the estimate): each user does 10 searches a day, each query has about 4 words and a word is about 5 characters, so a query is about 20 bytes (1 byte per character). For every typed character the client sends a request, so a search of 20 characters means about 20 requests. Then the request rate is 10 million x 10 queries x 20 characters / 24 hours / 3,600 seconds, which is about 24,000 queries per second. The peak is about twice that: 48,000 QPS.

For data growth: if 20% of the daily queries are new, the new data per day is 10 million x 10 queries x 20 bytes x 20% = 0.4 GB. This is small. The hard part of this design is not storage but speed: tens of thousands of lookups per second, each within a few milliseconds.

Requirements

RequirementValue
SuggestionsReal-time, as the user types
ResultsTop 5, sorted by popularity
Users10 million DAU
Peak loadAbout 48,000 QPS
AvailabilityHigh, no downtime on failures
Data growthAbout 0.4 GB per day

✨ Features

  • Top 5 suggestions in under 100 ms.
  • 10 million DAU and about 48,000 peak QPS.
  • About 0.4 GB of new data per day.

✅ Benefits

  • Shows that the load is about speed, not storage.
  • Peak QPS guides cache and server sizing.
  • The numbers justify a precomputed structure.

⚠️ Problems

  • The per-user assumptions can be wrong in real life.
  • Peaks can be higher during events.
  • Each keystroke is a request, so debouncing is important.

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Step 1: Understanding the Problem

Requirements

  1. Real-Time Suggestions: Display relevant matches as the user types.
  2. Top-k Results: Return up to 5 results sorted by popularity.
  3. Scalability: Handle 10 million DAU with a peak QPS of 48,000.
  4. High Availability: Handle failures without system downtime.

Interview questions and answers

Estimate the QPS of an autocomplete service.
With 10 million users doing 10 searches of 20 characters each, there are about 2 billion requests a day, about 24,000 per second on average and about 48,000 at peak.
How much new data grows every day?
About 0.4 GB, assuming 20% of the daily queries are new.
Cross question: How can the client reduce the number of requests?
Wait a short time (debounce) after typing before sending, cache earlier results in the browser, and do not send for very short prefixes if not useful.
Cross question: Why is this a speed problem and not a storage problem?
The data is small (a few GB per day), but each lookup must return in milliseconds at tens of thousands per second.

🧩 Step 2: High-level design: data gathering and query service

Hinglish samajh: System do services mein bantata hai: data gathering service queries ko jama karke batati hai ki har query kitni baar search hui (frequency table), aur query service prefix lekar sabse popular 5 queries deti hai. Saral tareeka SQL ka LIKE aur ORDER BY frequency DESC LIMIT 5 hai, par badi table par ye bahut dheema hai, isliye trie chahiye.

The system is broken into two services. The data gathering service collects the queries users type and aggregates them to know how often each query is searched. The query service takes a prefix and returns the top 5 most popular queries that start with it.

Here is the simplest version. The data gathering service stores each query and its frequency in a frequency table. When a user searches for "twitter", the frequency of "twitter" is increased by one (or the row is created). (Doing this in real time for every query is not practical for large datasets, but it is a good starting point to explain the idea; we improve it later.) Example frequency table: twitter 35, twitch 29, twilight 25, twin peak 21, twitch prime 18, twitter search 14, twillo 10 and so on.

The query service uses this table. For the prefix "tw" it can run a query like SELECT * FROM frequency_table WHERE query LIKE 'tw%' ORDER BY frequency DESC LIMIT 5. This works for a small data set, but when the table is huge, scanning and sorting the matches is too slow for 48,000 requests per second. That is why we need a better data structure, the trie, which comes next.

A frequency table (example)

QueryFrequency
twitter35
twitch29
twilight25
twin peak21
twitch prime18
twitter search14
twillo10

The basic (slow) query

␀class="nu">0␀
SELECT query
FROM   frequency_table
WHERE  query LIKE 'tw%'
ORDER  BY frequency DESC
LIMIT  class="nu">5;

␀class="nu">1␀
␀class="nu">2␀

✨ Features

  • Two services: data gathering and query.
  • A frequency table of queries.
  • Ranking by frequency.

✅ Benefits

  • Simple to explain and build.
  • Separates writes (collecting data) from reads (answering).
  • A starting point for the optimized design.

⚠️ Problems

  • Real-time updating of the table is not practical at scale.
  • The LIKE query is slow on large tables.
  • Every request sorts matches.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Step 2: High-Level Design + Data Gathering Service + Query Service

At the high-level, the system is broken down into two services:

  1. Data Gathering Service:
    • Collects user queries and aggregates them for frequency analysis in real-time.
    • Real-time processing is not practical for large data sets; however, it is a good starting point
  2. Query Service: Provides the top-k suggestions based on the user’s input.
  • Aggregates query data from analytics logs and updates the frequency table.
  • Processes historical data weekly to build a trie (prefix tree).
  • Uses the frequency table from data gathering service.
  • Processes user input and retrieves top-k suggestions from the frequency table using a Trie.
  • Optimized for fast lookups using caching and efficient data structures.
  • For example when a user types “tw” in the search box, the following top 5 searched queries are displayed.

Interview questions and answers

What are the two services in the design?
The data gathering service collects and aggregates queries into frequencies, and the query service returns the top 5 matches for a prefix.
Why is the simple SQL approach not enough?
A LIKE query with ORDER BY has to scan and sort many rows for each request, which is too slow at tens of thousands of requests per second.
Cross question: Why separate gathering from querying?
Collecting data can be slow and batched, while answering must be instant. Separating them lets each be optimized differently.
Cross question: How would an index help the basic query?
A prefix index helps find matching rows, but sorting by frequency for each prefix is still costly. A trie with cached top results avoids that.

🌳 Deep dive: the trie data structure

Hinglish samajh: Trie ek tree hai jisme har node ek akshar hai aur root se kisi node tak ka raasta ek prefix batata hai. Ek jaise shuruaat wali queries ek hi raasta share karti hain, isliye ye compact hai. Top k nikalne ke teen kadam: prefix node dhundo, uske neeche ke saare queries nikalo, aur frequency se sort karke top k lo. Ye dheema ho sakta hai, isliye do sudhaar: prefix ki lambai par limit (jaise 50) aur har node mein top k queries ko cache karna, taaki traversal aur sorting ki zaroorat hi na pade.

A trie (pronounced "try", from retrieval) is a tree used to store strings. Each node represents a character, the path from the root to a node spells a prefix, and each node has up to 26 children (one per letter, in our lowercase-only case). A node can also mark "a complete query ends here" and store the frequency of that query. Because queries with the same start share the same path, the trie is compact: "tree", "try" and "true" all share the path "t" - "r".

To get the top k most searched queries for a prefix, do three steps: (1) find the prefix node by walking from the root following the letters typed; (2) traverse the subtree below that node to collect all the valid queries; (3) sort them by frequency and take the top k. This is correct, but it can be slow: if the prefix is short (like "t"), the subtree may contain millions of queries.

Two optimizations fix the speed. First, limit the maximum length of a prefix: users rarely type a very long search (say longer than 50 characters), so the walk to the prefix node costs at most about 50 steps, which is a constant. Second, cache the top k queries at each node: store the five most popular queries right in every node, so that once you have the prefix node, the answer is already there with no traversal and no sorting. This uses more memory but turns the lookup into about O(length of prefix), which is tiny.

The trie is rebuilt from fresh data periodically (weekly in this chapter), so it is not updated query by query. In addition, a filter layer can remove unwanted suggestions (for example hateful or dangerous queries). Because it is a separate layer, you can change the filtering rules without rebuilding the trie, and unwanted entries are deleted from the database asynchronously.

How it works, step by step

  1. Walk from the root following the typed letters to the prefix node (at most about 50 steps).
  2. Read the top k queries cached in that node.
  3. Return them to the client.

Example queries and frequencies (illustration, k = 2)

QueryFrequencyPath in the trie
tree10t - r - e - e
try29t - r - y
true35t - r - u - e
toy14t - o - y
wish25w - i - s - h
win50w - i - n

Top 2 cached at some nodes (from the queries above)

Prefix nodeCached top 2
ttrue (35), try (29)
trtrue (35), try (29)
totoy (14)
wwin (50), wish (25)
wiwin (50), wish (25)

✨ Features

  • A tree of characters that shares common prefixes.
  • Frequency stored at the end of each query.
  • Top k cached at each node; prefix length limited.

✅ Benefits

  • Very fast lookups: depends on prefix length, not on data size.
  • Compact storage for many similar strings.
  • Easy to cache and to shard by prefix.

⚠️ Problems

  • Caching top k in every node uses extra memory.
  • The trie must be rebuilt to include new data.
  • A filter layer is needed to remove unwanted suggestions.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Trie Data Structure

The trie is a tree-like data structure used to store and retrieve query strings efficiently.

Key Features
  1. Compact Storage: Represents prefixes hierarchically to minimize redundancy.
  2. Frequency Information: Stores the popularity of queries at each node.
  3. Steps to get top k most searched queries
  • Find the prefix
  • Traverse the subtree from prefix node to get all valid children
  • Sort the children and get top k
  • Optimizations:
    • Cache top-k queries at each node to speed up retrieval and avoid traversing the whole trie.
  • Limit prefix length to reduce search space as users rarely type a loong search query (say 50).
Trie Operations
  1. Create:
    • Built weekly using aggregated query data.
    • The source of data is from Analytics Log/DB.
  2. Update: Rarely updated in real-time; weekly updates replace old data.
  3. Delete:
  • Filters remove unwanted or harmful suggestions (e.g., hate speech).
  • Having a filter layer gives us the flexibility of removing results based on different filter rules.
  • Unwanted suggestions are removed physically from the database asynchronically.

Interview questions and answers

What is a trie and why use it for autocomplete?
A tree where each path from the root spells a prefix. It lets us find the node of any prefix quickly and share storage for common prefixes. It is a natural fit for prefix-based suggestions.
How do you get the top k suggestions from a trie?
Find the prefix node, then either traverse its subtree and sort (slow), or read the top k that were precomputed and cached in the node (fast).
Cross question: Why limit the prefix length?
Users rarely type very long queries (say beyond 50 characters). Limiting the length bounds the walk to a small constant number of steps.
Cross question: How do you remove harmful suggestions?
Put a filter layer in front of the results with configurable rules, and delete the entries from the database asynchronously, instead of changing the trie directly.

⚡ The query flow and speed optimizations

Hinglish samajh: Query flow: user prefix bhejta hai, service trie mein prefix node dhundti hai, node mein cached top k milta hai, aur chhota JSON response wapas jaata hai. Speed ke liye: har node mein top k cache, prefix ki lambai par limit, AJAX requests (page refresh nahi) aur browser caching (jaise Cache-Control max-age=3600), taaki same prefix par browser dobara request na bheje.

Putting the trie to work, the query flow has three simple steps. (1) Prefix search: the user types a letter; the client sends the current prefix to the API servers (through a load balancer); the service finds the prefix node in the trie. (2) Top-k selection: because each node caches its top k queries, there is no need to traverse the subtree or sort anything. (3) Response construction: the cached results are put into a response and returned quickly, usually as a small JSON list.

The notes list four optimizations that make this fast. Cache at each node (the trie stores the top k in every node, avoiding repeated work). Limit the prefix length to a small maximum (say 50). AJAX requests: in web apps, the browser sends the request in the background with AJAX, so the page does not refresh and the suggestions appear smoothly. Browser caching: for many applications the autocomplete suggestions do not change much within a short time, so the server can tell the browser to cache the answer (for example with a Cache-Control header; Google uses max-age = 3600 seconds), and the browser then reuses the result for the same prefix without asking again.

A cacheable response (HTTP)

GET /autocomplete?q=tw HTTP/class="nu">1.class="nu">1

HTTP/class="nu">1.class="nu">1 class="nu">200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: private, max-age=class="nu">3600     ␀class="nu">0␀

[␀class="nu">1␀, ␀class="nu">2␀, ␀class="nu">3␀, ␀class="nu">4␀, ␀class="nu">5␀]

✨ Features

  • Find the prefix node, read cached top k, return.
  • Limit prefix length; cache at each node.
  • Use AJAX and browser caching.

✅ Benefits

  • Responses in a few milliseconds.
  • Fewer requests reach the servers.
  • A smooth experience without page refreshes.

⚠️ Problems

  • Browser-cached results may be a little out of date.
  • Memory use grows with cached top-k lists.
  • Per-keystroke requests still need debouncing on the client.

Interview questions and answers

Describe the query flow.
The client sends the current prefix; the service finds the prefix node in the trie, reads the cached top k, and returns them as a small response.
What optimizations make autocomplete fast?
Caching top k in each trie node, limiting prefix length, using AJAX requests, and browser caching with a Cache-Control header.
Cross question: Why is browser caching useful here?
Suggestions for a given prefix change slowly, so the browser can reuse an answer for a while and save a network request.
Cross question: What does debouncing do?
The client waits a short moment after the last keystroke before sending, so it does not send a request for every single character during fast typing.

🏭 Deep dive: the data gathering pipeline

Hinglish samajh: Har search par trie update karna practical nahi hai (billions queries). Isliye raw queries analytics logs mein jaati hain (append-only), aggregators unhe frequency table mein badalte hain (aam taur par hafte mein ek baar), workers naya trie banate hain aur trie database mein rakhte hain, aur trie cache uska snapshot lekar tezi se serve karta hai. Trie ko document store mein snapshot ke roop mein ya key-value store mein (prefix = key, top results = value) rakh sakte hain.

Earlier we said we update the table on every search. At real scale this is not practical. Users enter billions of queries per day, so updating the trie on each query would be far too slow, and the top suggestions do not change much once the trie is built anyway. So the design is changed: instead of updating in real time, we collect data into logs, aggregate it in batches and rebuild the trie periodically.

The pieces: Analytics logs store the raw search queries. They are append-only and not indexed; this is just a stream of raw events. Aggregators turn the raw logs into weekly aggregated data (a frequency table). How often to aggregate depends on the use: for real-time applications such as Twitter, you aggregate over a shorter interval; for most others, once a week is good enough. Aggregated data is a table of query, time and frequency. Workers are servers that run asynchronously at set intervals to build the trie and store it in the trie database. The Trie cache is a distributed cache that keeps the trie in memory for fast reads, and it takes a weekly snapshot of the database. The Trie database is the persistent storage.

There are two storage options for the trie database. A document store (for example MongoDB): since a new trie is built weekly, we can periodically take a snapshot, serialize it and store the serialized data. A key-value store: the trie can be represented as a hash table, mapping each prefix to a key and the data on each trie node (the top results) to the value. The key-value form makes it very easy to look up one prefix.

How it works, step by step

  1. Searches are appended to the analytics logs.
  2. Aggregators summarize the logs into frequencies (weekly for most uses).
  3. Workers build a new trie from the aggregated data.
  4. The trie is stored in the trie database.
  5. The trie cache takes a snapshot of the database for fast serving.

Components of the pipeline

ComponentRole
Analytics logsRaw query events, append-only and not indexed
AggregatorsTurn logs into frequency tables (weekly for most uses, shorter for real-time use cases)
WorkersAsynchronous jobs that build the trie at set intervals
Trie databasePersistent storage (document store snapshot or key-value store)
Trie cacheDistributed in-memory copy of the trie for fast reads

Key-value form of the trie (example, k = 2)

Key (prefix)Value (cached top results)
ttrue (35), try (29)
trtrue (35), try (29)
trutrue (35)
wwin (50), wish (25)

✨ Features

  • Append-only logs, batch aggregation and asynchronous workers.
  • Trie stored as a snapshot or in a key-value store.
  • Trie cache for fast reads.

✅ Benefits

  • No heavy work on the query path.
  • Simple and robust batch processing.
  • Easy to rebuild or roll back a trie version.

⚠️ Problems

  • New trending queries appear only after the next rebuild.
  • Rebuilding a huge trie takes resources.
  • Weekly data can be stale for fast-changing topics.

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Data Gathering Pipeline

In the high-level design, whenever a user types a search query, data is updated in real-time. This appraoch is not practical.

  • Users may enter billions of queries per day. Updating the trie on every query is not feasible.
  • Top suggestions may not change much one the trie is built.
Updated Design
  1. Analytics Logs:
    • Stores raw query data as logs for weekly aggregation.
    • Logs are append-only and are not indexed
  2. Aggregators:
    • Process logs into frequency tables, suitable for trie construction.
    • For real-time applications such as Twitter, aggregate data in a shorter time interval.
    • For other cases, aggregating data less frequently, say once per week is good enough.
  3. Workers:
    • Asynchronous servers rebuild the trie and store it in persistent storage.
  4. Storage Options:
    • Trie Cache: Trie Cache is a distributed cache system that keeps trie in memory for fast read.
    • Trie DB
      1. Document Store (e.g., MongoDB): Since a new trie is built weekly, we can periodically take a snapshot of it, serialize it, and store the serialized data in the database like MongoDB
      2. Key-Value Store:
        • Maps prefixes to node data for fast access.
        • Every prefix in the trie is mapped to a key in a hash table.
        • Data on each trie node is mapped to a value in a hash table.

Interview questions and answers

Why not update the trie on every search?
There are billions of queries a day, so real-time updates are too heavy, and top suggestions rarely change much once the trie is built.
Describe the data gathering pipeline.
Raw queries go to analytics logs, aggregators summarize them into frequencies, workers build a new trie and store it in the trie database, and the trie cache loads a snapshot for fast serving.
Cross question: How would you store the trie persistently?
Either serialize a snapshot into a document store such as MongoDB, or store it as a key-value table where each prefix is a key and the cached top results are the value.
Cross question: How often should you aggregate?
For real-time use cases such as Twitter, in a shorter interval. For most other cases, weekly is good enough.

🧱 Scalability: sharding the trie

Hinglish samajh: Trie ek server ke liye bahut bada ho sakta hai aur 48,000 requests per second ek server nahi sambhal sakta, isliye trie ko shard karte hain: pehle akshar (ya do aksharon) ke range ke hisaab se alag servers par. Par angrezi mein sab aksharon par barabar queries nahi hoti, isliye shard map manager asli data ke distribution ko dekhkar ranges tay karta hai (jaise "s" ko alag shard).

The trie may become too big for one server, and one server cannot handle 48,000 requests per second. So we shard the trie: split it across several servers. The simplest rule is by the first letter(s): the first server holds prefixes that start with "a" to "m", and the second holds "n" to "z". With 26 letters we can go further, using up to 26 servers by first letter, and beyond that by the first two letters ("aa" to "ag" on one server, "ah" to "an" on another, and so on).

But the distribution is not even. Many more English words start with "c" than with "x", so splitting by alphabet range alone gives some servers much more data than others. The solution is a shard map manager: it looks at the actual data and analyzes the historical distribution of queries, then decides the ranges. For example, if the letters "s" take as many queries as "u" to "z" combined, then "s" gets its own shard and "u-z" share another. A request first asks the shard map manager which server holds the prefix, then goes to that server.

Sharding by prefix range (example)

ServerPrefix rangeReason
Shard 1a to mA simple alphabet split
Shard 2n to rBalanced with the data volume
Shard 3sThe letter "s" has as many queries as several other letters together
Shard 4t to zRemaining letters grouped together

✨ Features

  • Shard the trie by prefix ranges.
  • Use a shard map manager based on the real data distribution.
  • Further split busy ranges (for example by two letters).

✅ Benefits

  • Each shard holds a manageable amount of data.
  • Requests are spread over several servers.
  • Hot letters can be split further.

⚠️ Problems

  • Uneven letter distribution needs analysis and maintenance.
  • The shard map manager must be highly available.
  • Rebalancing shards means moving data.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Scalability

  1. Sharding:
    • Distribute trie nodes across servers based on prefix ranges (e.g., a-m, n-z).
    • Further shard within prefixes to balance uneven distributions (e.g., aa-ag, ah-an).
  2. Load Balancing:
  • Use a shard map manager to route requests to the appropriate server.

Interview questions and answers

How do you scale the trie across servers?
Shard it by prefix ranges (for example a-m and n-z), and split busier ranges further, using a shard map manager to route requests.
Why is a simple a-to-z split not enough?
Letters are not equally common, so some shards would hold far more queries than others. The ranges must follow the real distribution.
Cross question: What does the shard map manager do?
It keeps the mapping from prefix ranges to servers, based on historical query data, and tells the service which shard to query.
Cross question: How would you make the autocomplete service highly available?
Replicate each shard on several servers, keep the shard map manager redundant, and let the load balancer skip failed nodes.

🌍 Advanced features: languages and trending queries

Hinglish samajh: Do extensions: multi-language support (trie ke nodes mein Unicode characters rakhna) aur country ke hisaab se alag tries banana. Trending queries ke liye hafte bhar ka rebuild bahut dheema hai, isliye haal ki queries ko zyada wazan do aur Kafka ya Spark Streaming jaise streaming systems se data lagatar process karo.

The notes close with two extensions. Multi-language support: our design works only with lowercase English letters. To support other languages, store Unicode characters in the trie nodes instead of just 26 letters (Unicode includes characters of all the world's writing systems). Nodes then need a different way to store children, such as a hash map instead of a fixed array of 26 slots. Also, users in different countries search for different things, so you can build separate tries for different countries, and use a CDN to bring each country's trie closer to its users.

Trending (real-time) queries: suppose a major event happens and everyone suddenly searches for it. A weekly rebuild would show it far too late. Handling this is hard, but a few ideas help: reduce the working data set by sharding; change the ranking model so that recent queries get higher weights (a query that was searched a lot in the last hour counts more); and use streaming systems (such as Apache Kafka or Spark Streaming) to process the data continuously instead of in weekly batches. These ideas are advanced, so mention them as possible directions.

Extensions

ExtensionProblemIdea
Multi-languageOnly 26 English letters are supportedStore Unicode characters in the trie nodes
Per-country resultsDifferent countries search different thingsBuild a separate trie for each country; serve it from a nearby cache or CDN
Trending queriesWeekly rebuilds are too slow for breaking newsWeight recent queries more; use streaming systems; shard to reduce the data set

✨ Features

  • Unicode support for many languages.
  • Country-specific tries.
  • Trending queries through weighting and streaming.

✅ Benefits

  • Works for a global user base.
  • Results feel local and relevant.
  • Fresh results for breaking events.

⚠️ Problems

  • Unicode tries are bigger and more complex.
  • Many tries increase storage and operational work.
  • Streaming pipelines are harder to build and run.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Multi-Language Support + Trending Queries

  1. Unicode Characters: Use Unicode to support non-English languages.
  2. Country-Specific Tries: Build separate tries for different countries or regions.
  • Handle real-time events by dynamically updating trie nodes or weighting recent queries more heavily.

Interview questions and answers

How would you support other languages?
Store Unicode characters in the trie nodes instead of only 26 letters, and use a map for children.
How would you handle trending queries?
Weight recent queries more heavily, process data with streaming systems instead of weekly batches, and shard to reduce the data set.
Cross question: Why build a trie per country?
Search behavior differs between countries, so country-specific suggestions are more relevant, and smaller tries are faster.
Cross question: What is the risk with trending queries?
Spam or manipulation can push low-quality or harmful queries to the top, so filtering and abuse detection become more important.

💻 Hands-on: a trie with cached top-k in code

Hinglish samajh: Code ka vichar saral hai: trie ko offline banao (queries aur frequencies insert karo, phir har node mein top k cache karo), aur online lookup mein sirf prefix ke akshar follow karke node ki cached list lauta do. Mehnat ka kaam build ke waqt hota hai, isliye query bahut tez chalti hai. Ye code aur udaharan meri taraf se hain.

To see how simple the core idea is, here is a small trie in C#. (The code and the example numbers are my own illustration, matching the example in the trie lesson with k = 2.) The trie is built offline: first we insert all queries with their frequencies, then a build step walks the trie and stores the top k queries in every node. Online, a lookup just walks the prefix and returns the cached list.

Notice how the work is split. All the expensive operations (inserting, collecting and sorting) happen during the build. The query path is only a short walk and a read, which is why it can be so fast. In a real system, the built trie would be serialized to the trie database and loaded into the trie cache on many servers.

Online and offline work

PhaseWorkCost
Offline buildInsert queries, collect all queries under each node, sort, keep the top kHeavy but done weekly in the background
Online lookupWalk at most 50 characters and read the cached listA few microseconds to milliseconds

A trie with cached top-k (C#)

public class TrieNode
{
    public Dictionary<char, TrieNode> Children = new();
    public int Frequency;                              ␀class="nu">0␀
    public List<(string Query, int Freq)> Top = new(); ␀class="nu">1␀
}

public class AutocompleteTrie
{
    readonly TrieNode root = new();
    const int K = class="nu">2, MaxPrefix = class="nu">50;

    public void Insert(string query, int freq)
    {
        var node = root;
        foreach (char c in query)
        {
            if (!node.Children.TryGetValue(c, out var next))
                node.Children[c] = next = new TrieNode();
            node = next;
        }
        node.Frequency = freq;
    }

    ␀class="nu">2␀
    public void Build() => Collect(root, ␀class="nu">9␀);
    List<(string, int)> Collect(TrieNode node, string prefix)
    {
        var all = new List<(string, int)>();
        if (node.Frequency > class="nu">0) all.Add((prefix, node.Frequency));
        foreach (var (c, child) in node.Children)
            all.AddRange(Collect(child, prefix + c));
        node.Top = all.OrderByDescending(x => x.Item2).Take(K).ToList();
        return all;
    }

    ␀class="nu">3␀
    public IEnumerable<string> Suggest(string prefix)
    {
        if (prefix.Length > MaxPrefix) prefix = prefix.Substring(class="nu">0, MaxPrefix);
        var node = root;
        foreach (char c in prefix)
            if (!node.Children.TryGetValue(c, out node)) return Array.Empty<string>();
        return node.Top.Select(t => t.Query);
    }
}

␀class="nu">4␀
␀class="nu">5␀
␀class="nu">6␀
␀class="nu">7␀
␀class="nu">8␀

✨ Features

  • Offline build fills the top-k lists.
  • Online lookup is a short walk.
  • Prefix length is limited.

✅ Benefits

  • Tiny query cost.
  • Easy to test with a few example queries.
  • The same structure can be sharded and cached.

⚠️ Problems

  • The build step uses extra memory.
  • This version holds the trie in one process only.
  • Updating a single frequency requires a rebuild of affected nodes.

Interview questions and answers

How would you implement the autocomplete lookup?
Build a trie offline with the top k queries cached in every node; at query time walk the typed prefix (limited length) and return the node's cached list.
What is the time complexity of a lookup?
O(p), where p is the prefix length (at most about 50), independent of the number of stored queries.
Cross question: How would you handle updates?
Rebuild the trie periodically from aggregated data, and publish the new version atomically so serving servers swap to it.
Cross question: How would you test it?
Insert a small set of queries with known frequencies, build, and check the suggestions for several prefixes, including prefixes that do not exist.
